summaries.example: Imagine a storybook that shows a whole parade on one page. We usually watch a parade one moment at a time: first one person walks by, then another. Some philosophers compare this with God’s supposed view of time: perhaps God does not wait for each moment, but knows the whole story at once. Other philosophers think God lives through moments, though God’s life may never end.
summaries.summary: The word “eternity” can mean God’s relationship to time, without deciding what that relationship is. Christian philosophers have explored two main ideas. Divine timelessness says that God is not in time, does not experience moments arriving one after another, and does not change. Divine temporality says that God is in time, experiences succession, and exists at every time. Some views combine parts of both ideas. For example, one proposal says God is timeless without creation but temporal in relation to the created world. Another says that God has a kind of time different from the measured time of human life. Supporters of timelessness argue that the most perfect being should not suffer the limits of ordinary time, and that timeless knowledge might avoid problems about knowing future choices. Supporters of temporality argue that knowing changing facts, acting in the world, remembering, deciding, and responding may require change. The entry explains that none of these arguments settles the issue for everyone. It also describes how Augustine, Boethius, Anselm, Aquinas, and other thinkers shaped the discussion, and how ideas about time in physics can enter the debate.
key_ideas: Christian thinkers have disagreed about whether God is timeless or lives through time.
A timeless God would not grow older or move from past to future. A temporal God would experience succession, meaning one moment following another.
The debate connects ideas about God’s knowledge, action, change, prayer, freedom, and the nature of time.
Some arguments use religious writings, while others begin with philosophy or with ideas from physics.
The entry also discusses eternity in questions about numbers, statements, and whether time is real.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because a view about God and time affects many other beliefs. It can change how people understand prayer, God’s knowledge of the future, human freedom, creation, change, and God’s relationship with the world. It also teaches an important philosophical lesson: a single word can hide several different questions, so we need careful definitions before comparing answers.

important_terms.definition: The question of how God is related to time. In this entry, the word does not choose between being outside time and living through time.
The idea that God does not live through one moment after another and does not change with time.
The idea that God is in time, lives through moments, and has no time at which God does not exist.
A belief that God knows everything, has unlimited power, is perfectly good, created the world, and remains active in it.

questions_to_think_about: If someone could see an entire journey at once, would that be the same as taking the journey?
Would a God who never changes still be able to answer a prayer or act in history?
Does knowing what someone will do make that person’s choice unfree?
Which seems easier to understand: a God outside time or a God living through endless time?

summaries.example: Suppose a person hears a piece of music. A human listener experiences its notes successively: one note occurs, then another, and memory connects them. A defender of divine timelessness may say that God’s life is not like this sequence; God possesses life without succession and knows temporal events in an atemporal present. A defender of divine temporality may reply that experience of succession need not involve human limitations. An omniscient temporal God could remember the entire past and know the future while still experiencing events in an ordered way.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what it could mean to call God eternal. It uses “eternity” as a neutral term for God’s relation to time, then contrasts divine timelessness with divine temporality. Timelessness is often understood as the absence of temporal succession and change, but its defenders differ over whether it involves a special kind of duration, an eternal present, or a relation in which temporal events are present to God. Temporality includes pure temporalism, in which God lives through an infinite temporal life, as well as intermediate views. These include relative timelessness, where God’s mode of time differs from measured human time; the view that God is timeless without creation but temporal with creation; and the proposal that God exists in time before time receives a measurable structure. The dispute draws on Christian scripture and historical theology, especially Augustine and Boethius, but it also uses metaphysics and physics. Arguments against timelessness claim that omniscience of tensed facts, causal action in history, and mental activities associated with personhood involve change. Arguments for timelessness claim that temporal existence has limitations, that timeless knowledge might help with foreknowledge and freedom, and that relativity theory may support a distinction between God and time. The entry emphasizes that each proposal faces serious conceptual questions, including how a timeless being can observe or cause temporal events. It finally notes that atemporality also appears in debates about propositions, mathematical objects, and whether time or spacetime is fundamental.
key_ideas: The debate concerns both whether God is located in physical spacetime and whether God’s life includes succession; these questions are related but not identical.
Historical discussions often distinguish timeless eternity from everlastingness, or existence through every time without a beginning or end.
Arguments against timelessness appeal to changing tensed facts, divine action and causal relations, and activities associated with personhood, such as deliberating or intending.
Arguments for timelessness appeal to divine perfection, the possibility of complete foreknowledge, and interpretations of relativity theory.
Proposals such as atemporal duration, relative timelessness, and timelessness without creation try to occupy positions between simple timelessness and simple temporality.
The source presents objections and replies rather than a final resolution.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question is not merely about a definition of “eternal.” It influences accounts of divine immutability, simplicity, omniscience, prayer, creation, providence, and human freedom. It also shows how philosophy of religion can depend on several fields at once: interpretation of religious sources, metaphysics of time, theories of knowledge and action, and physical theories of spacetime. Studying the debate helps readers separate distinct claims that are often run together, such as being outside physical spacetime and lacking temporal experience.

important_terms.definition: In this entry, God’s relationship to time in general. The term is used neutrally between timelessness and temporality.
The view that God is not located in time and that God’s life has no succession. Different versions disagree about how a timeless God relates to temporal events.
The view that God is in time, typically experiences succession, and exists at every time. It includes several forms, not just the idea that God is temporal exactly as humans are.
The relation of earlier and later among events. A being that experiences succession experiences events in an ordered sequence.
The view that all times or events are equally real and that temporal reality can be completely described without fundamental facts such as “it is now noon.”
A family of views holding that time has a metaphysically privileged present or other tensed facts, such as the fact that a particular moment is now.
An approach that reasons from the idea that God is the greatest or most perfect possible being to conclusions about divine attributes.

A proposed relation between something eternal and something temporal. It is meant to explain how a timeless God and events in time could be present together without making all temporal events simultaneous with one another.

questions_to_think_about: If God knows a changing tensed fact, does God’s knowledge change, or can the same reality be known without succession?
Can a timeless being genuinely act, respond, or enter causal relations with a temporal world?
Does divine perfection favor timelessness, or could a temporal life contain goods such as music, action, and relationship?
Can divine foreknowledge and human freedom be reconciled by saying that God knows events timelessly?
What, if anything, does relativity theory show about the relation between time and timelessness?

summaries.example: Think about a live sports game. A fan in the stands sees the game play by play: the score changes, and each new moment arrives. Now imagine a coach watching a recording with a timeline and knowing every play. The coach still watches in order, but has a complete record. Philosophers ask whether God is more like a viewer who sees all moments together, as timelessness suggests, or more like a participant who lives through moments, as temporality suggests. They also ask whether either kind of knowledge allows God to act and whether people can still choose freely.
summaries.summary: “Eternity” has several meanings in Christian thought. In this entry, it means God’s relationship to time without taking sides between the main options. Divine timelessness says that God is not in time, does not experience succession, and does not change. Divine temporality says that God is in time and experiences a sequence of moments; one common version says that God exists at every time forever. Other positions are more complicated. God might have a kind of time unlike the measured time of the universe, or God might be timeless without creation and temporal in relation to creation. The historical background includes Plato, Aristotle, Philo, Plotinus, Augustine, Boethius, Anselm, Aquinas, and medieval Jewish and Islamic thinkers. Boethius described eternity as possessing an unlimited life all together, while Augustine explored the difficulty of understanding time and God’s relation to it. Philosophers who oppose timelessness argue that an omniscient God would know changing facts, that acting in history and responding to prayer involve relations with temporal events, and that remembering or deciding may require change. Philosophers who defend timelessness argue that temporal life includes limits such as loss, incomplete knowledge, and dependence on the passage of time. They also argue that timeless knowledge may help address the apparent conflict between divine foreknowledge and human freedom. The entry examines these arguments and their objections without declaring one view victorious.
key_ideas: The entry treats eternity as an open question about God’s relation to time, not as a synonym for only timelessness.
Timelessness and temporality each have several versions, including views that combine timeless and temporal features.
A major disagreement concerns whether changing knowledge, action, or mental activities require God to be in time.
Supporters of timelessness connect it with perfection, immutability, and a possible solution to problems about foreknowledge and freedom.
Supporters of temporality argue that God’s involvement with a changing world may require temporal relations or changes.
The debate uses ideas from Christian history, philosophical theories of time, and modern discussions of spacetime.
summaries.why_it_matters: A person’s view of God and time can affect ideas about prayer, freedom, creation, change, and divine knowledge. The discussion also connects religious questions with theories about whether the present is special and with scientific accounts of spacetime. Most importantly, it demonstrates why philosophers distinguish questions carefully: being outside physical spacetime is not automatically the same as lacking succession, and existing forever is not automatically the same as being timeless.

important_terms.definition: A neutral word for God’s relation to time. It can refer to either being timeless or existing through every time.
The position that God is outside time, does not experience one moment after another, and does not undergo change in the ordinary temporal way.
The position that God exists in time and experiences succession. In many versions, God exists at every time without beginning or end.
The view that time includes facts about what is happening now, such as “it is noon,” and that these facts can genuinely change.
The view that events are ordered by earlier and later, but that no one moment is fundamentally more real or present than another.
The idea that God knows everything that can be known, including truths about temporal events and human choices.
The claim that God’s nature does not change. Some philosophers connect this with timelessness.
The approach of asking what properties a greatest possible being would have, then using those properties in reasoning about God.

questions_to_think_about: Does knowing every event at once differ from knowing events one after another?
If God creates the universe, does that action make God change or enter time?
Can an unchanging being remember, plan, decide, or answer a request?
Would a temporal God necessarily have the same limitations that human beings have?
How might the A-theory and B-theory lead to different views about divine knowledge?
